title: Management, O&M, leases and affermage; PPP types and names
objectives: Explain when a contract to manage existing infrastructure or a service can be a service PPP, and when it cannot.
Distinguish management contracts, conventional O&M contracts and financial leases from PPPs.
Explain why privatisation, regulated utilities, public domain concessions and partial divestiture are not PPPs.
Classify PPPs by source of revenue, ownership, scope and financing, and use the terms greenfield, brownfield and yellowfield.
Recognise the main names used for PPPs, including BOT, PFI, concession, lease and affermage.

sections.heading: 1. Service PPPs: “at-risk” long-term management contracts
2. Management contracts, O&M contracts and financial leases
sections.body:
**Management contracts** are **not long-term** like PPPs and are **less complex**. They use private expertise for service design and delivery, operations control, staffing and equipment procurement.

- The private contractor takes some responsibilities but **does not assume commercial risk**.
- The **public sector keeps ownership** of the assets, which are usually existing assets.
- The contractor is **paid a fee**, typically on a **performance basis** with payment and penalty schemes. Its profit may be at some risk, but little or no capital is at stake.
- There is **no significant private capital investment**. So efficiency gains are **more limited**, and there are **no disciplinary mechanisms** such as **lenders' due diligence** or capital exposed to performance risk.
- They usually last **two to five years**, sometimes longer for complex facilities such as **ports or airports**.
- They can be **politically and socially more acceptable** (for example in water). They are useful when the **private sector will not invest**, or when the government does **not want a long-term commitment**.

The UN ESCAP models include **supply or service contracts**, **maintenance management** and **operational management**.

**Conventional O&M contracts** are usually based on **cost-plus** and/or pay for **inputs rather than results**, under **highly prescriptive** documents. They are **not PPPs**, but they are **suitable in many contexts** and offer **flexibility**.

**Financial lease contracts** are long-term contracts in which assets are provided in return for **periodic lease payments**. Compared with PPPs, they transfer **much less risk**, and **no significant management or performance responsibility**. They are **purely financial** arrangements, typically used for **tax benefits** or **lower financing costs**. They are **not expected** to improve service performance.

**Monetising existing assets (Box 1.10).** A government may own a profitable user-pays asset, such as a toll road, airport or port. It may **lease or concession** it for a long term, transferring **O&M, life-cycle cost management and the revenue rights**, usually for an **upfront fee**. This is **asset monetisation**, and the Guide treats these contracts as **private finance PPPs**. Their value depends on a **fair price** and above all **how the proceeds are used**. A clear, well-communicated plan helps win public consent. An example is the **Chicago Skyway** lease ($1.83 billion). **Asset recycling** means reinvesting such proceeds in new or existing infrastructure. It may use PPPs, but also other structures such as securitisation or an outright sale.

sections.heading: 3. Privatisation and regulated markets are not PPPs
sections.body:
Section 2.4 of the Guide covers private involvement that happens **outside procurement**.

**Privatisation.** In its strict sense, privatisation is the **permanent transfer** of a public asset and service responsibility. The Guide is clear: **privatisations are not PPPs**. Table 1.1 shows the differences:

| Privatisation | PPP |
|---|---|
| The private sector owns the **full property** of the asset | The **government** is normally the legal owner, and the asset is **handed back** at the end |
| **No contract** in strict terms; conditions are set by **sector regulation** | A **detailed contract** sets each party's rights and obligations |
| Time to operate is **unlimited** | Time is **limited by contract** |
| **No strict alignment of objectives**; the provider sets quantity, quality and price, although KPIs may be imposed by regulation | The **government specifies** the quantity and quality of service |
| **More freedom to set prices**, subject to market and regulatory rules | The partner receives the **agreed price** or user charges, with little or no flexibility |

Privatisation is typical in **telecoms and energy** when a government **liberalises** a sector: it sells its monopoly company to private investors, sometimes after splitting it to boost competition.

**Regulated investor-owned utilities.** In many countries, utilities such as electricity and telecoms can be **owned outright** by private firms. Like a user-pays PPP, they charge users. But they are **not procurement methods**. The government is not contracting for a specific asset. It **grants a right to run a business** under regulated conditions for an **unlimited time**. In such liberalised markets, **no contracts are needed** for new infrastructure, because each operator has a **natural incentive** to invest at its own risk.

**Public authorisations and public domain concessions.** A private promoter may be **authorised** to build and run an asset under **regulated conditions**. An example is a renewable energy producer that buys land and sells power under a **subsidised** regime. There is **no contract** and no direct government requirement, so this is **not a PPP**. But if a **public counterparty commits to pay** for the power and **tenders a DBFOM** for the plant under a **Power Purchase Agreement (PPA)**, it **is a PPP**. A **public domain concession** grants the use of land for a long time, possibly up to **99 years**, for example to develop port facilities, and the land **reverts** to the government at the end. It is **not a PPP**, because there is no contract and the government is a **passive regulator**, not an active contract manager.

**Partial divestiture.** Selling **shares** of a public operator, often through an **Initial Public Offering (IPO)** on the stock market, is a “**partial privatisation**”. Management does not change, and there is **no contract** and no private control of the service. It is **not a PPP**. An example is Spain's airport operator **AENA** in 2014.

**Putting it together (Table 1.2).**

| PPP feature | DB | DBF | DBOM | User-pays DBFOM | Gov-pays DBFOM/PFI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Formal contract | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Long-term | No | Sometimes | Normally | Yes | Yes |
| DB and O&M bundled | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Life-cycle risk transfer | No | No | Sometimes | Usually | Usually |
| Private finance | No | Yes | No | Yes | Yes |
| Pay linked to performance/use | No | No | Sometimes | Yes (use) | Yes (performance) |

sections.heading: 4. Types and variations of PPPs
sections.body:
Section 3.1 organises PPP types by **four factors**:

1. **Source of funds for the partner's revenue**: **user-pays** (mainly charges to users) versus **government-pays** (mainly government payments). This is the **most relevant classification**.
2. **Ownership of the SPV**:
   - **conventional PPPs**: 100% private;
   - **institutional PPPs**: publicly owned (100% public), or a JV or *empresa mixta* where the **public party controls** the company;
   - **other JVs or *empresas mixtas***.
3. **Scope or object of the contract**:
   - **infrastructure PPPs**: significant capital investment to develop and manage infrastructure;
   - **integrated PPPs**: infrastructure **plus the right and obligation to operate a service**;
   - **O&M PPPs or service PPPs**: **no capital investment** and no new infrastructure by the partner.
4. **Relevance of private financing**: **co-financed or hybrid PPPs**, with a material portion of **public finance**, usually grants, versus **conventional PPPs**.

PPPs can also be described by the **past use of the site**, using terms common among investors:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Greenfield** | Investment in **new** infrastructure, a DBFOM recently awarded or under construction |
| **Brownfield** | Investment in assets that **existed before procurement**, or earlier greenfields that are now **in operation** |
| **Yellowfield** (secondary stage) | Investment in **significant renewals, refurbishment or substantial expansion** of existing infrastructure |

The Guide notes that other uses of “greenfield” and “brownfield” exist (see the Glossary). In the exam, use the Guide's meanings.

sections.heading: 5. The many names for private finance PPPs
sections.body:
The **same type of PPP** can have **different names** in different countries or sectors. This is due to legal tradition, legislation or common language. **Any** contract under these names is a private finance PPP **as long as the PPP features are present** (Table 1.3).

- **DBFOM, DBFM, DCMF, DBFO.** These names **describe the functions** transferred. For the Guide they are all **synonyms for a private finance PPP**, and can be user-pays or government-pays. Sometimes “maintain” is **implicit** in “operate” (DBFO), or “O” is dropped when there is no user interface. Remember that **DBOM has no private finance**, so it is **not** a private finance PPP.
- **BOT, BOOT, BTO, ROT.** These names focus on **legal ownership and control** of the asset. In many **civil code** countries, the private partner cannot fully own the asset in legal terms. It is only the **economic owner**, and the asset stays in the **public domain**. So these acronyms can be **confusing**. **BTO** means legal ownership is private **only during construction**. **ROT** (Rehabilitate-Operate-Transfer) replaces “build” with **rehabilitate**. The Guide treats them all as **synonyms of the DBFOM group**.
- **BOO / ROO.** The private sector **builds, owns and operates** a facility and **sells the product or service** to users. ROO is the same, but for the **rehabilitation** of existing assets.
- **PFI (Private Finance Initiative).** The **UK** name, used mainly for **government-pays DBFOM**. It is essentially a BOT paid by **availability payments**, or by **capacity charges** in the case of IPPs.
- **Concession (of public works).** A traditional **civil code** legal term. It is the legal title that lets the government transfer **economic rights of use** in a public asset. It was originally for **user-pays DBFOM**. Some countries (for example **Chile and Spain**) also use it for **government-pays** contracts, while others keep it for user-pays only.
- **Arrendamiento (leasing of public works).** A civil code option for buildings when the land is **disposable real estate**, not land reserved for public use. It is a **private contract under civil law**, although the tender stays under public law.
- **PPP / APP as a legal term.** Some civil code countries use PPP in law for **government-pays** DBFOMs, usually where **most revenue comes from the budget** (also the ESA 2010 approach). **Brazil** uses it for DBFOMs with **any** public payment.
- **Hybrid PPPs.** These combine **concessional financing** with private investment to cover a project's **government support** needs and improve **affordability**.
- **Joint ventures / empresas mixtas**, **institutional PPPs**, and the EBRD's **public service contract plus project support agreement** are also listed. Mixed equity companies are **rarely seen** in government-pays schemes.

sections.heading: 6. Names for service PPPs: leases, affermage and others
sections.body:
Table 1.4 lists names used for PPPs that relate **only or mainly to managing existing infrastructure or operating public services**.

| Name | What it means in the Guide |
|---|---|
| **Concession (of services)** | An O&M-type contract with **no material investment**, generally used where **most revenue comes from users**, often for public utilities. It is also used to contract out an existing road or airport for an **upfront fee** (“**monetisation**”). |
| **Lease** | Like a concession, a legal institution granting **economic rights** or **economic ownership** of an asset. It is most common for O&M of **existing** infrastructure and **user-pays** PPPs. In some countries a lease means the **government keeps capital expenditure**, and the partner only does ordinary maintenance and operation. |
| **Affermage** | A **French** term for contracting out the right to operate existing infrastructure. The **operator keeps its fee from the receipts** and **pays the rest to the authority**. It may include some CAPEX. It is **never linked to government-pays** contracts. |
| **Service contract** | In **civil code** law, a transfer of the **operation of a public service** in the strict sense (such as water or passenger transport). In **common law** countries it has no specific legal meaning and covers many, usually **short**, outsourcing contracts. **Only a few** are PPPs. |
| **Management contract** | Often an O&M contract focused on the **long-term maintenance** of assets, or a “service only” contract (especially in water). It is a PPP **only if** it is long-term, carries risk and is performance oriented. |

For **O&M contracts**, the Guide says only a **few** “deserve” to be called PPPs. They need to be **clearly long-term**, with some **life-cycle cost management** transferred, **cost-related risk** transferred and a clear **performance orientation**. An O&M contract may take on PPP attributes when it requires **substantial CAPEX**.

**Key points (Box 1.12):**

- DBFOM-type names describe **functions**. BOT-type names describe **ownership**. Ownership is **not at the heart** of a PPP, as long as the asset is public or is transferred back at the end.
- Names such as **lease, affermage and concession** describe the **legal title** to use and operate the asset.
- O&M, management and service contracts are PPPs **only with long-term risk transfer** and pay linked to **performance or demand**.
- The **main classification** is **user-pays versus government-pays**. Some countries link the first with **concessions** and the second with **PFI**.

example.title: Sorting the Eastvale water and energy contracts
example.body:
Imagine the fictional city of Eastvale reviews five arrangements.

1. **A 3-year contract** for a private firm to operate the water treatment plant. The firm is paid its actual costs plus 8%. This is **not a PPP**. It is short term and **cost-plus**, so almost no risk is transferred. It is a conventional O&M contract.
2. **A 12-year contract** to manage the water network, paid a fixed annual fee with deductions if leakage and billing KPIs are missed. The firm also takes over major maintenance. This can be a **service PPP**: it is long-term, performance-oriented and transfers risk.
3. **A 30-year affermage** of the existing water system. The operator collects tariffs, keeps its operator fee and pays the rest to the city. It can be a **user-pays service PPP** under a French-style legal title, as long as the operator carries real risk and has clear performance duties.
4. **A wind farm developer** buys private land and sells power under the national renewable subsidy regime. There is no contract with the city. It is **not a PPP**, but a regulated authorisation.
5. **The city tenders** a 25-year contract to design, build, finance and operate a solar plant, and a public utility commits to buy the power under a **PPA**. This **is a PPP**, similar in scope to a DBFOM.

Notice that the label (lease, affermage, O&M) never decides the answer by itself. The features do.

examTraps.trap: Assuming any management or O&M contract is a service PPP.
examTraps.fix: It must be long-term (usually 7+ years; below 5 is short), transfer significant risk and be performance-oriented. Cost-plus or input-based contracts are not PPPs.

examTraps.trap: Confusing privatisation or regulated utilities with user-pays PPPs.
examTraps.fix: Both may charge users, but privatisation and regulated utilities have no procurement contract, unlimited time and full private ownership. A PPP is a time-limited contract with hand-back.

examTraps.trap: Treating every renewable power project as a PPP.
examTraps.fix: A regulated authorisation with subsidised prices and no contract is not a PPP. A tendered DBFOM with a public offtaker under a PPA is a PPP.

examTraps.trap: Thinking affermage or leases can be government-pays.
examTraps.fix: Affermage is never linked to government-pays contracts. The operator keeps its fee from user receipts and pays the rest to the authority. Leases are also mostly user-pays.

examTraps.trap: Mixing up greenfield, brownfield and yellowfield.
examTraps.fix: Greenfield means new assets. Brownfield means assets already existing or in operation. Yellowfield (secondary stage) means significant renewal, refurbishment or expansion of existing assets.

keyTerms.meaning: A long-term, at-risk, performance-oriented contract to manage existing infrastructure or provide a public service.
Payment of actual costs plus a margin rather than a pre-agreed amount; it transfers little or no risk.
A usually short (2–5 year) contract paying a fee to manage services or assets, with no commercial risk and no significant private investment.
A long-term arrangement providing assets for periodic lease payments, used for tax or financing benefits, with little risk or management transfer.
Leasing or concessioning an existing revenue-earning asset to a private partner, usually for an upfront fee.
A privately owned utility running a business under regulation for an unlimited period; not a procurement method.
A long-term grant of public land for a regulated use, such as a port, without a PPP contract; not a PPP.
A French term for contracting out the operation of existing infrastructure, where the operator keeps its fee from receipts and pays the rest to the authority.
Private Finance Initiative; the UK name mainly for government-pays DBFOM PPPs.
New infrastructure / existing or operating infrastructure / significant renewal or expansion of existing infrastructure.

summary: Management or service contracts can be service PPPs only if they are long-term, transfer significant risk and are performance-oriented; cost-plus pay rules this out.
Management contracts, conventional O&M contracts and financial leases are not PPPs, but they can still be useful tools.
Long-term leases or concessions of profitable existing assets (asset monetisation) are private finance PPPs.
Privatisation, regulated utilities, public authorisations, public domain concessions and partial divestiture are not PPPs, because there is no procurement contract.
PPPs are classified by revenue source (the main classification), SPV ownership, scope and the relevance of private finance.
DBFOM-type names describe functions, BOT-type names describe ownership, and concession, lease and affermage describe legal title; all are PPPs only if the features are present.
Affermage is never government-pays; PFI is mainly government-pays; concession is mainly, but not always, user-pays.

slides.title: When a service contract is a PPP
points: Transfers significant risk
Performance oriented
Relatively long term: seven years or more may do
Cost-plus pay means not a PPP
slides.narration: Welcome to the last lesson on PPP scope. Not every PPP builds something new. A contract to manage existing infrastructure, or to run a service, can be a service PPP. But it needs three things. It must transfer significant risk, it must be focused on performance, and it must be fairly long. The Guide says contracts under five years are short term. Ten years is commonly seen as long term, and seven years or more may be enough, but that is a judgement. One quick disqualifier: if the partner is simply paid its actual costs plus a margin, very little risk moves, so it is not a PPP.

slides.title: Management contracts and O&M
points: Management contracts: usually two to five years
Fee-based, no commercial risk, no private capital
Conventional O&M: inputs, cost-plus, prescriptive
Useful and flexible, but not PPPs
slides.narration: Management contracts bring private expertise into running a service, but they are not PPPs. They usually last two to five years. The contractor earns a fee, often with bonuses and penalties, but takes no commercial risk and invests no significant capital. That means no lenders checking the project, and fewer efficiency gains. Conventional O&M contracts are similar. They often pay for inputs, or on a cost-plus basis, with very detailed specifications. Don't dismiss them, though. O&M contracts are flexible, and management contracts can be more politically acceptable, for example in the water sector.

slides.title: Leases and asset monetisation
points: Financial leases: purely financial, little risk transfer
Monetisation: lease a profitable asset for upfront fee
Monetisation contracts are private finance PPPs
Value depends on price and use of proceeds
slides.narration: Two kinds of lease can confuse you. A financial lease is a purely financial arrangement, used for tax benefits or cheaper finance. It moves little risk and no real management responsibility, so it is not a PPP. Asset monetisation is different. A government leases a profitable existing asset, such as a toll road, to a private partner for a long period, usually for a large upfront fee. The partner takes over operations, life-cycle costs and revenue. The Guide treats these as private finance PPPs. Whether they give value depends on a fair price and on what the government does with the money.

slides.title: Privatisation is not a PPP
points: Full private ownership versus hand-back
Regulation versus a detailed contract
Unlimited time versus contract term
Provider sets price versus agreed price
slides.narration: Let's compare privatisation and PPP side by side. In a privatisation, the private company owns the asset outright. In a PPP, the government normally stays the legal owner, and the asset is handed back at the end. A privatised firm follows sector regulation, while a PPP partner follows a detailed contract. Privatisation has no time limit. A PPP ends when the contract ends. And a privatised firm has more freedom to set prices and service levels, while in a PPP the government specifies the service and the price is agreed in the contract.

slides.title: Other arrangements outside procurement
points: Regulated investor-owned utilities
Renewable authorisations with subsidised prices
Public domain concessions, up to 99 years
Partial divestiture through share sales
slides.narration: Some other arrangements look like PPPs but are not. Regulated investor-owned utilities, such as private electricity or telecom companies, run a business under regulation with no time limit. A wind developer selling power under a subsidy regime has an authorisation, not a contract. But if a public body tenders a plant and commits to buy the power under a power purchase agreement, that is a PPP. Public domain concessions of land, for example for a port, leave the government as a passive regulator. And selling shares in a public company is a partial privatisation.

slides.title: Four ways to classify PPPs
points: Revenue source: user-pays or government-pays
Ownership: conventional, institutional, joint venture
Scope: infrastructure, integrated, O&M or service
Finance: co-financed or hybrid versus conventional
slides.narration: The Guide classifies PPPs using four factors. First and most important, where the revenue comes from: users, or the government. Second, who owns the project company: fully private in a conventional PPP, publicly controlled in an institutional PPP, or shared in a joint venture. Third, the scope: an infrastructure PPP, an integrated PPP that also runs a service, or an O&M or service PPP with no capital investment. Fourth, how much public money is involved: co-financed or hybrid PPPs, versus conventional ones. Investors also talk about greenfield, brownfield and yellowfield projects.

slides.title: Same PPP, many names
points: DBFOM family describes functions
BOT family describes ownership
PFI: UK name for government-pays
Concession: civil code legal title
slides.narration: Around the world, the same PPP can have many names. DBFOM, DBFM and DBFO describe what the partner does. BOT, BOOT and similar names describe who owns the asset and when it is transferred. But in many civil code countries the partner can't legally own public assets, so those names can confuse. PFI is the United Kingdom's name, mainly for government-pays contracts. Concession is a civil code legal title, traditionally for user-pays, though Chile and Spain also use it for government-pays. The key idea: a name never makes a PPP. The features do.

slides.title: Leases, affermage and service contracts
points: Lease: economic rights, mostly existing user-pays assets
Affermage: operator keeps fee, pays rest
Affermage is never government-pays
Only a few O&M contracts deserve PPP status
slides.narration: Finally, the names for service PPPs. A lease gives the partner economic rights over an existing asset, and is mostly used for user-pays arrangements. Affermage is a French term. The operator collects the receipts, keeps its operator fee, and pays the rest to the authority. Remember that affermage is never used for government-pays contracts. A service contract has a precise meaning in civil code law, but in common law countries it just means outsourcing. And for O&M contracts, the Guide says only a few deserve to be called PPPs. Well done. You've completed the scope of PPPs.

quiz.question: Which set of conditions makes a contract to manage existing infrastructure a service PPP under the Guide's broad definition?
options: It includes private finance and is paid by users
It transfers significant risk, is performance-oriented and has a relatively long term
It is awarded without competition to an experienced operator
It is paid on a cost-plus basis over at least ten years
quiz.explanation: Service PPPs need significant risk transfer, performance orientation and a relatively long term. A cost-plus contract transfers little risk, so it is never a PPP, however long it lasts.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements. 1: Contracts below 5 years are generally regarded as short term. 2: A 10-year contract is commonly regarded as long term.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: The Guide says contracts below 5 years are generally short term and 10 years is commonly long term. Seven years and above may be enough for service PPPs, as a matter of judgement.

quiz.question: Which statement about management contracts is correct according to the Guide?
options: The private contractor usually assumes full commercial risk
The contractor is paid a fee and does not assume commercial risk
They normally require significant private capital investment
They always last longer than 15 years
quiz.explanation: In management contracts, the contractor earns a fee, often performance-based, and takes no commercial risk. There is no significant private capital, and they are usually two to five years long.

quiz.question: Why is a financial lease contract not regarded as a PPP?
options: Because it transfers little risk and no significant management or performance responsibility
Because it is always shorter than five years
Because the lessor is always a state-owned bank
Because it is paid by users rather than the government
quiz.explanation: Financial leases are purely financial arrangements used for tax or financing benefits, and they do not transfer significant risk or management responsibility. They are in fact long-term contracts.

quiz.question: Which of the following arrangements IS regarded as a PPP by the Guide?
options: A renewable developer selling power under a general subsidy regime with no contract
A 99-year public domain concession of port land under regulation
An IPO selling shares of the state airport operator
A tendered DBFOM of a power plant with a public offtaker under a Power Purchase Agreement
quiz.explanation: A tendered DBFOM with a committed public buyer under a PPA is a PPP. The other three have no procurement contract: they are a regulated authorisation, a public domain concession and a partial privatisation.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a feature of privatisation rather than of a PPP?
options: The asset is handed back to the government when the contract expires
A detailed contract sets out the rights and obligations of each party
The time to operate the asset is unlimited
The government specifies the quantity and quality of service
quiz.explanation: In a privatisation, the time to operate is unlimited and the private sector owns the asset. Hand-back, a detailed contract and government-specified service are PPP features.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: A PPP investment in the significant refurbishment or substantial expansion of existing infrastructure is described as ____.
options: yellowfield or secondary stage
greenfield
brownfield
asset recycling
quiz.explanation: Yellowfield (secondary stage) refers to significant renewals, refurbishment or expansion. Greenfield means new assets, and brownfield means assets already existing or in operation.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the factors the Guide uses to classify types of PPP?
options: Source of funds for the partner's revenue
Ownership of the SPV
The legal tradition of the country, civil code or common law
Scope or object of the contract
quiz.explanation: The Guide classifies PPPs by revenue source, SPV ownership, contract scope and the relevance of private financing. Legal tradition affects the names used for PPPs, not the classification of PPP types.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes how affermage works?
options: It is a UK term for government-pays DBFOM contracts
It is always used for new infrastructure with large capital investment
The authority pays the operator a fixed availability fee from its budget
The operator keeps its fee from user receipts and pays the remainder to the authority
quiz.explanation: Affermage is a French term for operating existing infrastructure, where the operator keeps its fee and passes on the rest. It is never linked to government-pays contracts; the UK government-pays term is PFI.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about PPP names. 1: BOT-type names focus on legal ownership and control of the asset. 2: DBFOM-type names include the word ownership in their definition.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: BOT, BOOT and similar names capture legal ownership, while DBFOM-type names describe functions and do not refer to ownership. Ownership is not at the heart of the PPP concept.

quiz.question: A city signs a 3-year contract for a private firm to maintain its street lights, paid a fixed fee with KPI deductions. Is it a service PPP under the Guide?
options: No; 2–4 years is too short to transfer cost and result risks
Yes; the pay is linked to KPIs, so it is performance-based
Yes; any contract for existing infrastructure is a service PPP
No; every service PPP must include private finance
quiz.explanation: The Guide says 2–4 years is not long enough for service management or maintenance to be a PPP, because risk linked to costs and results cannot be properly transferred (Ch 1 §2.3). Service PPPs do not need private finance.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about leases (Table 1.4). 1: Leases are more commonly seen with O&M contracts on existing infrastructure, mostly in user-pays PPPs. 2: In some countries, 'lease' is reserved for contracts where the private partner is responsible for all capital expenditure.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Table 1.4 says leases are mostly used for O&M contracts on existing infrastructure, normally user-pays. In some countries 'lease' is reserved for contracts where the government stays responsible for capital expenditure, so statement 2 is false.

quiz.question: A 15-year contract to run a city's bus depot pays the operator its actual costs each year plus a 6% margin. Why is it not a PPP?
options: Fifteen years is too short for any service PPP
Bus services can never be procured as PPPs
The operator does not own the depot buildings
Cost-plus pay transfers little, if any, risk to the operator
quiz.explanation: None of the Guide's service PPP examples is a PPP if pay is on a cost-plus basis, because it transfers little, if any, risk (Ch 1 §2.3). Length is not the problem here, and a 15-year bus concession is one of the Guide's examples.

quiz.question: A 15-year bus concession requires the partner to renew a few buses each year. Why is it treated as a service PPP rather than a DBFOM?
options: Bus services never need any capital investment at all
The partner does not collect any fares from passengers
The initial investment is relatively small and the main cost is annual
Its term is too short for any DBFOM-type contract
quiz.explanation: The Guide says such contracts are management or service contracts because the initial investment is relatively small and the predominant cost is annual. Where initial investment is significant, the contract could easily be a private finance PPP.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements. 1: A management contract with a significant initial investment could easily be classified as a private finance PPP. 2: Whether a contract is a PPP is a question of degree and judgement.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Both are true. The Guide says classifying a contract as a PPP is a matter of degree and judgement, and significant initial investment can make it a private finance PPP (Ch 1 §2.3).

quiz.question: Why does the Guide say management contracts give more limited efficiency gains than PPPs?
options: The contractor is always paid on a cost-plus basis for its work
Little private capital is at stake, so lenders' due diligence is missing
The public sector gives up ownership of the assets it manages
They must run for longer than the useful life of the assets
quiz.explanation: Management contracts involve no significant private capital, so they lack disciplinary mechanisms such as lenders' due diligence and capital exposed to performance risk (Ch 1 §2.3). The public sector keeps ownership.

quiz.question: A government wants private expertise in its water utility, but the public dislikes private investment and the government does not want a long-term commitment. Which option does the Guide suggest may be useful?
options: A 30-year user-pays concession
A full privatisation by share sale
A management contract
An asset monetisation lease
quiz.explanation: Management contracts can be politically and socially more acceptable, for example in water, and are useful when there is no long-term commitment or no private willingness to invest. The other options are long-term or permanent.

quiz.question: Which best describes a conventional O&M contract, according to the Guide?
options: Long-term and performance-based, with life-cycle risk transferred
Financed by the operator and repaid by availability payments
Often cost-plus or input-based, under highly prescriptive documents
Based on an upfront fee paid for the rights to user revenue
quiz.explanation: Conventional O&M contracts are usually based on cost-plus and/or pay for inputs rather than results, under highly prescriptive documents (Ch 1 §2.3). Long-term risk transfer and performance focus describe a service PPP.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about conventional O&M contracts. 1: They are not regarded as PPPs. 2: The Guide says they should be avoided because they lack flexibility.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Conventional O&M contracts are not PPPs. But the Guide says they are suitable in many contexts and have the advantage of flexibility.

quiz.question: A government owns a profitable toll road. It grants a 40-year concession that transfers O&M, life-cycle costs and toll revenue rights, for a large upfront fee. How does the Guide treat this contract?
options: As a privatisation, since revenue rights move
As a private finance PPP (asset monetisation)
As a management contract with no real risk
As a financial lease used for tax benefits
quiz.explanation: Box 1.10 treats long-term leases or concessions of existing user-pays assets for an upfront fee as private finance PPPs. The asset is not permanently sold, so it is not a privatisation.

quiz.question: According to the Guide, what above all decides whether an asset monetisation gives value for the government?
options: What is done with the proceeds
How long the lease term is
How many bidders take part
Which legal title is used
quiz.explanation: Box 1.10 says value depends on a fair price and, above all, what is done with the proceeds, such as new infrastructure or less debt. A clear plan for the proceeds also helps public consent.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about asset recycling. 1: Asset recycling always uses PPP structures. 2: Brownfield PPPs can be part of an asset recycling programme.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Brownfield PPPs can be part of asset recycling, but it can also use non-PPP structures such as securitisation of revenues or outright sale of assets (Box 1.10).

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the other ways listed in the Guide for a government to capture value when it monetises an asset?
options: An upfront fee plus a minority stake in the project company
A yearly fee, fixed or as a percentage of revenue
A shorter lease term so the asset comes back sooner
Guaranteeing the partner a minimum return on equity
quiz.explanation: Box 1.10 lists an upfront fee plus a minority stake, a yearly fee, and a shorter lease term. A return guarantee would give value away rather than capture it.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: In its strictest sense, privatisation means ____.
options: any form of private management of public services, including all PPPs
the permanent transfer of a public asset and service responsibility to the private sector
a time-limited contract that ends with hand-back of the asset to government
the sale of a minority of a public company's shares on the stock market
quiz.explanation: Strictly, privatisation is the permanent transfer of a public asset and the duty to deliver the service. Using the word broadly to include PPPs is exactly the confusion the Guide warns against (Ch 1 §2.4).

quiz.question: In a privatised company, who mainly sets the quality, quantity and price of the service?
options: The private provider, within market and regulatory rules
The government, through a detailed output specification
The lenders, through the covenants in their loans
The users, through a vote at the annual meeting
quiz.explanation: Table 1.1 says in privatisation the private providers set quality, quantity and price, although regulation may impose KPIs or price rules. Detailed government specification is a PPP feature.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about Table 1.1. 1: KPIs may be imposed on a privatised company through regulation. 2: A concession may include a buyback provision reflecting fair market value at the end of the term.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Both are true. The Guide notes that KPIs can be imposed on a privatised entity by regulation, and that a concession could include a buyback provision at fair market value (Table 1.1).

quiz.question: In which sectors does the Guide say privatisation is typical?
options: Hospitals and schools, when budgets are tight
Rail, when fares are kept low for social reasons
Prisons and courts, when capacity is too short
Telecoms and energy, when a sector is liberalised
quiz.explanation: The Guide gives telecoms and energy as typical examples: a government liberalises the sector and sells its monopoly company, sometimes after splitting it. Social infrastructure is usually procured through contracts.

quiz.question: Why are regulated investor-owned utilities NOT procurement methods, according to the Guide?
options: They never charge users for the electricity or telecom services they provide
They are always owned by state enterprises rather than private investors
The government grants a right to run a business under regulation, for an unlimited time
They are paid availability payments by the sector regulator each month
quiz.explanation: The public sector is not contracting for a specific asset; it authorises a private business under regulated conditions with no time limit (Ch 1 §2.4). Like user-pays PPPs, these utilities do charge users.

quiz.question: Why is a 99-year public domain concession of port land NOT a PPP?
options: Its term is longer than any PPP is allowed to last
The land never reverts to the government at the end
There is no contract and the government is a passive regulator
Port facilities can never be procured as PPPs
quiz.explanation: The Guide says public domain concessions are not PPPs because there is no contract and the government acts as a relatively passive regulator, unlike a PPP where it actively manages a contract. The land does revert at the end.

quiz.question: A state sells 49% of its airport operator's shares through an IPO. The company's management does not change. How does the Guide classify this?
options: An institutional PPP under public control
A partial privatisation, which is not a PPP
A joint venture, which counts as a PPP
An asset monetisation, which is a PPP
quiz.explanation: A share sale is a partial privatisation or divestiture. There is no contract in the strict sense and private investors do not control the service, as in the AENA case in 2014 (Ch 1 §2.4).

quiz.question: In the Guide's comparison of contract types (Table 1.2), which feature does a DBOM have but a DBF does not?
options: Finance provided by the private sector
A formal contract between the parties
Design-build and O&M bundled in one contract
Revenues linked to use by the users
quiz.explanation: Table 1.2 shows DB and O&M bundled in DBOM but not in DBF. DBF has private finance and DBOM does not; both have a formal contract.

quiz.question: Which scope type does the Guide use for a PPP where the partner develops infrastructure and also has the right and obligation to operate a service?
options: An infrastructure PPP
An integrated PPP
An O&M or service PPP
An institutional PPP
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1 calls these integrated PPPs. An infrastructure PPP focuses on developing and managing the asset, a service PPP has no capital investment, and 'institutional' refers to ownership, not scope.

quiz.question: Under the ownership factor in Section 3.1, how does the Guide describe a conventional PPP?
options: An SPV that is 100% privately owned
An SPV controlled by the public party
An SPV with material public equity and board votes
An SPV wholly owned by a state enterprise
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1 lists conventional PPPs as 100% private ownership. Public control makes it institutional, and a material public stake with board votes makes it a joint venture.

quiz.question: Which PPP classification does the Guide call the most relevant?
options: Greenfield versus brownfield
User-pays versus government-pays
Conventional versus institutional
Infrastructure versus service
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the main classification is by the source of the partner's revenue: user-pays versus government-pays (Section 3.1 and Box 1.12). The others are secondary ways of describing PPPs.

quiz.question: Under the Guide's 'relevance of private financing' factor, what makes a PPP co-financed or hybrid?
options: Public and private shareholders in the same SPV
A material portion of public finance, usually grants
A mix of bank loans and bonds in the financing
Both construction and O&M included in the scope
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1 defines co-financed or hybrid PPPs as schemes with a material portion of public finance, usually grants. Shared public and private ownership falls under the ownership factor instead.

quiz.question: An investor buys a stake in a toll road PPP that has been open and operating for eight years. In the investor industry's terms, what is this investment?
options: Brownfield
Greenfield
Yellowfield
Asset recycling
quiz.explanation: Brownfield covers assets that existed before procurement or earlier greenfields that are now in operation. Greenfield means new assets under construction or recently awarded, and yellowfield means significant renewal or expansion.

quiz.question: When the name DBFO is used for a PPP, what is usually true about maintenance?
options: Maintenance stays with the government's own staff
Maintenance is paid on a cost-plus basis
Maintenance is left out of the contract scope
Maintenance is treated as implicit in 'operate'
quiz.explanation: Table 1.3 says that when DBFO is used, the 'maintain' function is sometimes considered implicit in operations. DBFO is still a synonym for a private finance PPP.

quiz.question: Why can BOT-type acronyms be confusing in many civil code countries?
options: Civil code law does not allow any private finance of public assets
Civil code countries do not allow the asset to be handed back
The partner is usually only the economic owner; legal ownership stays public
In those countries BOT always means a government-pays contract
quiz.explanation: In many civil code countries full legal ownership by the partner is not possible; the asset stays in the public domain and the partner is only the economic owner (Table 1.3). So names built on 'own' and 'transfer' can mislead.

quiz.question: In a BTO contract, when is legal ownership of the asset on the private side?
options: Only during operation
For the whole contract term
Only after the hand-back
Only during construction
quiz.explanation: Table 1.3 says BTO refers to contracts where legal ownership is on the private side only during construction. The Guide treats BTO as a synonym of the DBFOM group.

quiz.question: What does the ROT name change compared with BOT?
options: It replaces 'operate' with 'own' for permanent private assets
It removes the transfer of the asset at the end of the term
It adds government finance in place of private finance
It replaces 'build' with 'rehabilitate' for upgrading existing assets
quiz.explanation: ROT (Rehabilitate-Operate-Transfer) simply replaces 'build' with 'rehabilitate', for contracts whose investment is rehabilitation or upgrading. It is still a synonym of the DBFOM group.

quiz.question: Which describes a BOO arrangement in the Guide's nomenclature?
options: The government builds and owns a facility, and the private sector only operates it
The private sector builds a facility and transfers it before it starts operating it
The private sector builds, owns and operates a facility and sells its output to users
The private sector rehabilitates an existing facility and returns it immediately
quiz.explanation: In a BOO the private sector builds, owns and operates the facility and sells the product or service to users or beneficiaries. Transfer before operation describes BTO, and rehabilitation describes ROO or ROT.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about the term concession. 1: Chile and Spain also use it for government-pays DBFOM contracts. 2: All civil code countries reserve it for user-pays contracts only.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Some civil code countries, for example Chile and Spain, use 'concession' for government-pays DBFOMs, while others keep it for user-pays only. So statement 2 is false (Table 1.3).

quiz.question: When can arrendamiento (leasing of public works) be used as a legal alternative to a government-pays DBFOM?
options: When the asset is a toll road that is fully funded by user charges
When the land is disposable real estate, not land reserved for public use
When the private partner will keep the asset permanently after the term
When the tender process is exempt from public procurement law
quiz.explanation: Table 1.3 says arrendamiento is used for buildings when the land is real estate the government can dispose of. The contract is a private civil law contract, but the tender stays under public law.

quiz.question: How does Brazil's legal use of the term PPP differ from the approach in ESA 2010?
options: Brazil uses PPP only for user-pays concessions
Brazil treats any DBFOM with any public payment as a PPP
Brazil requires most revenue to come from the budget
Brazil does not use PPP as a legal term at all
quiz.explanation: Under ESA 2010, and in many civil code laws, the legal term PPP applies where most revenue comes from the budget. Brazil treats any DBFOM with any level of public payment as a PPP (Table 1.3).

quiz.question: What is a hybrid PPP, as defined in Table 1.3 of the Guide?
options: A single contract that combines a lease title with an affermage title
An SPV owned half by the state and half by private investors
A PPP that switches from user-pays to government-pays during the term
Concessional financing combined with private investment to cover government support needs
quiz.explanation: Table 1.3 describes hybrid PPPs as combining concessional financing with private investment, partly or fully covering the project's government support needs and improving affordability. Shared ownership describes a joint venture.

quiz.question: In the EBRD's 'public service contract plus project support agreement' structure, what does the project support agreement do?
options: It transfers legal ownership of the water network to the EBRD
It records the authority's commitment to the EBRD to cover revenue shortfalls
It sets the tariffs that users must pay for the whole term
It appoints the EBRD as the private operator of the service
quiz.explanation: The project support agreement is signed by the procuring authority with the EBRD and contains a direct commitment to cover the financial revenue shortfall, often as service payments linked to performance (Table 1.3).

quiz.question: Which describes a 'concession of services' in the Guide's Table 1.4?
options: An O&M-type contract with no material investment, mostly funded by users
A DBFOM contract for new works paid mainly by availability payments
A permanent sale of a public utility company to private investors
A long grant of public land for a regulated use, such as a port
quiz.explanation: Table 1.4 says a concession of services is an O&M-type contract with no significant investment, generally where most revenue comes from users, often for utilities. It can also be used for monetisation of an existing road or airport.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about service contracts. 1: In civil code law, the term usually refers to transferring the operation of a public service such as water. 2: In common law countries, the term has a specific legal meaning linked to PPPs.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: In civil code jurisdictions a service contract means transferring the operation of a public service. In common law countries it has no specific legal meaning and covers many short outsourcing contracts, and only a few are PPPs (Table 1.4).

quiz.question: According to the Guide, what can give an O&M contract the attributes of a PPP?
options: Payment on a cost-plus basis
A term of two to four years
Highly prescriptive input specifications
A requirement to invest substantial CAPEX
quiz.explanation: Table 1.3 says an O&M contract can have PPP attributes when it requires substantial CAPEX, in addition to long term, life-cycle and cost risk transfer, and performance focus. Cost-plus pay and short terms point the other way.

quiz.question: Which group of PPP names is based mainly on the legal title to use and operate the asset?
options: DBFOM, DBFM and DBFO
BOT, BOOT and BTO
Greenfield, brownfield and yellowfield
Lease, affermage and concession
quiz.explanation: Box 1.12 says lease, affermage and concession describe the legal title granted to use and operate the asset. DBFOM names describe functions, BOT names describe ownership, and the 'field' terms describe the past use of the site.
